text_blocks.snippet: High blood pressure (hypertension) is often called a "silent killer" because it typically does not cause any symptoms. Most people with high blood pressure feel completely fine and can live with it for years without knowing it.
snippet_highlighted_words: typically does not cause any symptoms

text_blocks.snippet: Symptoms During Dangerously High Levels (Hypertensive Crisis)

Symptoms usually only appear when blood pressure becomes severely elevated (often above 180/120 mm Hg). Seek emergency care immediately if extremely high blood pressure is accompanied by any of these warning signs:

list.snippet: Sudden vision changes (such as blurred or double vision)
Confusion, dizziness, or neurological changes (such as numbness, weakness, or difficulty speaking)

text_blocks.snippet: In some cases, people with elevated or rising blood pressure may occasionally notice mild or subtle signs, though these are not always reliable indicators of hypertension:

list.snippet: Fatigue or feeling tired all the time
Blood spots in the eyes (subconjunctival hemorrhage)
Headaches, particularly early in the morning

text_blocks.snippet: Because symptoms are rare, checking your blood pressure regularly is the only way to detect hypertension. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the American Heart Association recommend routine checks at least once a year if you are an adult, or as advised by your healthcare provider. You can also review detailed blood pressure categories and guidelines on the Mayo Clinic High Blood Pressure Overview.
